stories.title: Compassion
stories.fortuneLine: The hoist was the safe hour. The chain was concern. You sent away the hands that knew the difference.
stories.body:
A traveler once fell into a pit lined with thorns and shale.

He cried out for days, but no voice answered until nightfall.

Then came a woman in white, silent as smoke.

She tended his wounds, left water and bread, and said: “Speak no word by daylight. Call for me only in the darkest hour.”

Each night she returned, carrying something new: rope, cloth, a pulley, a length of carved wood.

But the traveler grew bitter. “If you truly cared,” he said, “you’d lift me out. You wouldn’t ask for patience.” She said nothing.

The next night, when she came with more tools, he turned his face from her and shouted, “I don’t want your kindness. I want freedom.”

So she climbed away, without a word, and did not return.

The following day he heard voices: men. They found him, pulled him out, and for a moment he thought he’d been saved. Then the chains came.

He had fallen inside royal hunting grounds. Trespass meant death.

As they bound him, a guard glanced down into the pit and muttered, “Someone was building a hoist.”

There, in the dirt, were the things she’d brought, each placed with quiet intent.

She had known. She had been helping in silence, waiting for the hour when it was safe. She was the king’s daughter.

And he had sent her away, before the dark was deep enough.
